First, I need to understand the geometry involved. Let's visualize triangle ABC, with side BC being extended to a point D. The external angle in this case would be angle ACD. The internal and opposite angles would be angles CBA (at point B) and BAC (at point A). 

The goal is to show that angle ACD is greater than both angles CBA and BAC. 

I recall from basic geometry that the sum of internal angles in a triangle is 180 degrees, or two right angles (which is consistent with one of the previous examples). Also, when a side of a triangle is extended, the external angle formed is equal to the sum of the two non-adjacent internal angles. 

So, angle ACD should be equal to the sum of angles CAB and CBA. Since angle ACD is the sum of these two angles, and each of these angles is less than 90 degrees (assuming a standard triangle), their sum should naturally be greater than each individual angle.

theorem example_thm (a b c d : Point) (AB BC CA : Line) (h1 : formTriangle a b c AB BC CA) (h2 : between b c d) : ∠ a:c:d > ∠ b:a:c ∧ ∠ a:c:d > ∠ a:b:c := by
  constructor
  case left =>
    -- Using the properties of angles in a triangle and the extension of side BC,
    -- we can show that the external angle ∠ a:c:d is greater than ∠ b:a:c.
    <;> simp_all [Point.onLine, Line.intersectsLine, Circle.onCircle, Triangle.ofPoints]
    <;> nlinarith [h1, h2]
  case right =>
    -- Similarly, we can show that the external angle ∠ a:c:d is greater than ∠ a:b:c.
    <;> simp_all [Point.onLine, Line.intersectsLine, Circle.onCircle, Triangle.ofPoints]
    <;> nlinarith [h1, h2]

nl_statement: For any triangle, when one of the sides is produced, the external angle is greater than each of the internal and opposite angles.Let $ABC$ be a triangle, and let one of its sides $BC$ have been produced to $D$. I say that the external angle $ACD$ is greater than each of the  internal and opposite angles, $CBA$ and $BAC$.  Let the (straight-line) $AC$ have been cut in half at (point) $E$ [Prop.~1.10]. <prf> Thus,  $ACD$ is greater than $BAE$. Similarly, by having cut $BC$ in half,  it can  be shown (that) $BCG$ ---that is to say, $ACD$---(is) also greater than $ABC$. Thus, for any triangle, when one of the sides is produced, the external angle is greater than each of the internal and opposite angles.
